title: A level Paper 3 mock — Set A: Microeconomics and macroeconomics
description: A synoptic Paper 3 drawing on all four themes. Section A is a data response on a regional airport (demand elasticity, exchange rates, contestability and aviation externalities); Section B is a data response on an energy price shock in a fictional economy (monetary policy, aggregate supply, oligopoly in energy retail and policy responses to external shocks). Each section has three data-response questions followed by a choice of 25-mark essay. Allow 2 hours: spend about 60 minutes on each section, including around 5 minutes reading the extracts and about 35 minutes on the essay. Use the data in every answer, draw diagrams where they help, and make sure your essay reaches a justified judgement.

questions.prompt: Using Table 1, calculate the price elasticity of demand for short-haul flights from Northmoor Airport between 2024 and 2025. Explain one reason why your figure may not be an accurate estimate of the price elasticity of demand.
questions.context:
Short-haul flying from Northmoor Airport (illustrative data)

Table 1: Short-haul flights from Northmoor Airport, 2022-2025 (illustrative data)
Year | Passengers (millions) | Average one-way fare (£) | Jet fuel price (US$ per tonne) | Exchange rate (US$ per £1) | Air Passenger Duty per short-haul economy passenger (£)

2023 | 6.2 | 66 | 900 | 1.24 | 13
2024 | 6.8 | 70 | 850 | 1.27 | 13
2025 | 6.5 | 77 | 820 | 1.15 | 15

Table 2: Share of short-haul passengers at Northmoor Airport by airline, 2025 (illustrative data)
Airline | Share of passengers (%)
Arrowjet | 46
Albion Air | 31
SkyBridge (entered 2023) | 15
Others | 8

Extract A: A busy airport with limited room
Northmoor Airport is a fictional regional airport in the north of England, owned by a private infrastructure fund. Its single runway is close to capacity at peak times, and take-off and landing slots at popular times are allocated mainly to airlines that used them in the previous season ('grandfather rights'). Arrowjet and Albion Air hold around 80% of the morning departure slots. In 2023 the low-cost carrier SkyBridge entered the market, leasing four aircraft rather than buying them, and offered fares around a quarter below those of the established airlines on its routes. Arrowjet responded by adding flights to the same destinations at similar times and matching SkyBridge's lowest fares on those routes. SkyBridge says it will withdraw from two of its four routes in 2026 because it cannot obtain enough morning slots to make them profitable.

Extract B: Costs, currency and passengers
For the airlines at Northmoor, fuel accounted for around 30% of operating costs in 2025. Fuel and aircraft leases are priced in US dollars, while most of the airlines' revenue at Northmoor is in pounds. Airlines buy some of their fuel up to a year in advance at agreed prices (hedging). In 2025 the pound fell against the dollar and airlines raised fares. Passenger numbers at Northmoor fell for the first time since 2021, even though the number of overseas visitors arriving through the airport rose by around 8%. Hotels and restaurants in the region reported their busiest summer for several years.

Extract C: Paying for pollution
Aviation creates carbon emissions, noise and local air pollution. Residents living under the flight path have campaigned against plans for a second runway, which the airport's owners say would create 3,000 jobs and bring £1.2 billion of private investment. The government has raised Air Passenger Duty (APD), a tax on each departing passenger, and is considering further increases. Airlines argue that APD is a blunt tool because it is charged per passenger rather than per tonne of carbon emitted, so a passenger on a modern, fuel-efficient aircraft pays the same as one on an older, less efficient aircraft. Some environmental groups favour a 'frequent flyer levy' that rises with the number of flights an individual takes each year, because a minority of people take a large share of all flights.
questions.mark_scheme:
Marking points:
1 mark for knowledge of the formula: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price.
1 mark for the percentage change in quantity: (6.5 - 6.8) ÷ 6.8 x 100 = -4.4% (accept -4.41%).
1 mark for the percentage change in price: (77 - 70) ÷ 70 x 100 = +10%.
1 mark for PED = -4.4 ÷ 10 = -0.44 (accept -0.4 to -0.45, sign may be omitted), with recognition that demand is price inelastic.
1 mark for one developed reason why the estimate may be inaccurate, applied to the context. For example: the ceteris paribus assumption does not hold, because other determinants of demand changed at the same time, such as the depreciation of the pound making holidays abroad more expensive for UK residents (Extract B), changes in real incomes, or SkyBridge's planned route withdrawals; or the figure uses an average fare across all routes, so it hides very different elasticities for business and leisure travellers; or it measures a single year's response, while demand is likely to be more elastic in the long run as passengers switch to other airports or rail.
A correct PED of -0.44 with no workings may be awarded the calculation marks; the explanation mark is awarded separately.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Depreciation: a fall in the value of a floating currency against another currency. A weaker pound raises the sterling price of imports and lowers the foreign currency price of UK exports, including services sold to overseas visitors.
Application: The pound fell from US$1.27 to US$1.15, a depreciation of around 9.4%. The dollar price of jet fuel fell from US$850 to US$820 per tonne (-3.5%), but in pounds it rose from around £669 to around £713 per tonne (+6.5%). Fuel is around 30% of operating costs and leases are also priced in dollars. Fares rose from £70 to £77 (+10%) and passengers fell from 6.8 million to 6.5 million, while overseas visitors rose by around 8% and regional hotels and restaurants had a busy summer.
Analysis: Airlines: costs priced in dollars rise in sterling terms, shifting their cost curves upward; with price-inelastic demand (PED of around -0.44) they can pass much of this on as higher fares, protecting revenue, but output falls and margins may be squeezed. UK residents face higher prices for holidays abroad (imports of services become dearer), so outbound demand falls. Local economy: overseas visitors find UK hotels, meals and attractions cheaper in their own currency, so inbound tourism (a service export) rises. Spending by visitors is an injection into the regional circular flow, raising incomes in hospitality and, through the multiplier, in supplying industries; some UK residents may also substitute 'staycations' for trips abroad. Overall, the impact shifts activity from airlines' outbound business towards the local visitor economy.
Evaluation: Hedging means much of the 2025 fuel cost was fixed in advance, so the full cost rise may only appear in 2026. The size of the effect depends on how long the depreciation lasts and on price elasticities (Marshall-Lerner condition and J-curve effects for the wider trade balance). The fall in passengers may also reflect the higher APD (£13 to £15) and SkyBridge's limited slots, not just the exchange rate. Visitors arriving by air also need airline seats, so airlines with routes from overseas may gain from inbound demand. The local multiplier may be small if much spending leaks out to national chains and imports.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 6 marks; Evaluation up to 2 marks.
Levels (Knowledge, Application, Analysis):
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated knowledge with little or no use of the data or context; analysis is absent or a list of assertions; any diagram is inaccurate or not used.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some reference to the data; one or two chains of reasoning that are partly developed; diagram broadly accurate but not fully integrated.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): Precise knowledge applied consistently to the context and figures; two clear, logical and well-linked chains of reasoning; accurate diagram fully explained and integrated where required.
Levels (Evaluation):
Level 1 (1 mark): A generic or asserted evaluative comment.
Level 2 (2 marks): A developed, supported evaluative point that is applied to the context (for example magnitude, time period or what the outcome depends on).
A* answer: Calculates the 9.4% depreciation and shows that fuel became dearer in pounds despite falling in dollars, links this to cost-push pressure on fares using the PED figure, contrasts falling outbound demand with rising inbound tourism and a regional multiplier, and evaluates using hedging, time lags and the other factors (APD, slots) that may explain the fall in passengers.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: A perfectly contestable market has no barriers to entry or exit and no sunk costs, so firms can enter, make profits and leave without loss ('hit-and-run' entry). The threat of entry forces incumbents to set prices close to average cost and to be efficient, regardless of the number of firms. Sunk costs, legal barriers and strategic barriers (limit pricing, predatory pricing) reduce contestability.
Application: Table 2 shows a three-firm concentration ratio of 92% (46 + 31 + 15) and a two-firm ratio of 77%, so the market is a highly concentrated oligopoly. SkyBridge entered in 2023 and reached a 15% share, leasing aircraft rather than buying them. Arrowjet and Albion Air hold around 80% of morning slots under grandfather rights. Arrowjet added flights and matched SkyBridge's lowest fares; SkyBridge is withdrawing from two of four routes. Average fares rose from £60 to £77 between 2022 and 2025 (+28%).
Analysis: Evidence for contestability: leasing means aircraft are not a sunk cost, because they can be returned or moved to another airport, so exit costs are low; SkyBridge's successful entry and 15% share show entry is possible; its fares a quarter below incumbents' suggest the threat of entry can hold down prices. Evidence against: slots are a scarce, legally allocated resource, so grandfather rights act as a legal barrier to entry, especially at profitable peak times; marketing, route launch costs and building brand recognition are sunk; Arrowjet's response looks like strategic, possibly predatory, behaviour that raises the risk of entry and deters future entrants; SkyBridge's planned exit shows entry may not be sustainable. If the market were contestable, incumbents would earn only normal profit in the long run; rising fares may indicate market power, which would lead to allocative inefficiency (P > MC).
Evaluation: Concentration does not by itself show a lack of contestability; the key is the height of barriers. Contestability varies by route and time of day: off-peak routes with spare slots may be highly contestable while peak routes are not. Fare rises may reflect higher costs (fuel in pounds, APD) rather than market power, so the fare data are not conclusive. The relevant market may be wider than one airport if passengers can use other airports or rail, which increases competitive pressure. Policy matters: auctioning or reallocating slots, or a second runway, could make the market far more contestable. A justified judgement might be that the market is only partially contestable: low capital sunk costs are outweighed by slot constraints and incumbents' strategic responses.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 8 marks; Evaluation up to 4 marks.
Levels (Knowledge, Application, Analysis):
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
Level 2 (3-5 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; relevant chains of reasoning that may be incomplete or one-sided; diagrams, if used, may contain minor errors.
Level 3 (6-8 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context and data; clear, logical and well-linked chains of reasoning covering more than one side of the issue, supported by accurate diagrams or calculations where relevant.
Levels (Evaluation):
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluation is generic or asserted, with little reference to the context; any judgement is unsupported.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Balanced evaluation supported by the data and context, weighing the significance of the arguments and reaching a justified judgement.
A* answer: Defines contestability precisely and separates it from concentration, uses the 92% CR3 and fare data, weighs low sunk costs from leasing against slot-based legal barriers and Arrowjet's strategic response, and concludes that contestability differs by route and time of day and depends on slot policy.

questions.mark_scheme:
This mark scheme covers both options. Mark the option the candidate has chosen using the indicative content for that option and the shared level descriptors.

OPTION (a): Air Passenger Duty and aviation externalities
Knowledge: Negative externalities of production and consumption; marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost; overproduction and welfare loss at the free-market output. Indirect specific tax; tax incidence; Pigouvian tax set equal to the marginal external cost. Alternatives: emissions trading (the UK ETS covers domestic flights and flights from the UK to the European Economic Area), carbon taxes on fuel, regulation (noise limits, night-flight bans, efficiency standards), a frequent flyer levy, subsidies for sustainable aviation fuel and rail, and limiting airport capacity.
Application: APD rose from £13 to £15 per short-haul passenger (Table 1); demand is price inelastic (PED of around -0.44); APD is charged per passenger, not per tonne of carbon (Extract C); a minority of people take a large share of flights; residents oppose a second runway; noise and local air pollution affect people under the flight path.
Analysis: A tax shifts the supply curve up by the amount of the tax, raising fares and reducing the number of flights towards the socially optimal level; with a diagram showing MSC above MPC, the tax internalises the externality and removes some or all of the welfare loss. Revenue can fund green investment or compensate affected residents. Because demand is price inelastic, the incidence falls mainly on passengers and the fall in passengers is small, but revenue is large. APD does not target carbon: it gives airlines no incentive to switch to efficient aircraft or sustainable fuels, so it is a poor match for the external cost. A carbon price per tonne or tradable permits would target emissions directly and create dynamic incentives to innovate. A frequent flyer levy would target the heaviest users, whose demand may be more income than price driven, and is more progressive. Regulation can deal with noise and night flights, which a tax on passengers does not target.
Evaluation: The size of the marginal external cost is hard to value, so the 'right' rate of APD is uncertain (government failure through information gaps). Inelastic demand limits the reduction in flights in the short run, but long-run demand is more elastic as alternatives such as rail develop. Carbon leakage: passengers may fly from airports abroad or transfer through foreign hubs, and higher APD may harm regional connectivity and tourism exports. Distributional effects: APD takes a larger share of income from lower-income occasional flyers than a frequent flyer levy. Combining instruments (permits for carbon, regulation for noise, APD as a revenue tool) may be most effective. A justified judgement on 'most effective' is needed, for example that APD is a useful revenue raiser but a weak externality tool compared with carbon pricing.

OPTION (b): A second runway and the macroeconomy
Knowledge: Aggregate demand (C + I + G + X - M); investment; the multiplier; long-run aggregate supply and productive capacity; current account (trade in services, including tourism); regional unemployment; macroeconomic objectives including environmental sustainability; conflicts between objectives.
Application: £1.2 billion of private investment and 3,000 jobs (Extract C); the runway is at capacity at peak times (Extract A); overseas visitors rose by around 8% (Extract B); northern England's regional economy; the UK's legally binding net zero target for 2050.
Analysis: Construction raises investment, shifting AD to the right; through the multiplier, real output and employment rise by more than the initial spending, particularly in a region with spare capacity. Once operating, extra capacity raises LRAS by improving connectivity for business, attracting foreign direct investment and supporting tourism, which increases potential growth (AD/AS diagram with LRAS shifting right). More inbound visitors raise service exports; but more outbound UK holidays raise service imports, so the net effect on the current account is uncertain. Lower fares from extra slots and new entrants raise real incomes and consumer surplus. Rebalancing growth towards the north may reduce regional inequality.
Evaluation: The size of the multiplier depends on leakages; much construction equipment and aircraft are imported. If the economy is near full capacity, the extra AD may be inflationary and crowd out other investment. The 3,000 jobs are a gross figure; displacement from other airports means net national job creation may be much smaller. Time lags: planning and construction could take a decade. Environmental costs (carbon, noise) conflict with net zero and may require offsetting policies; the social return may be lower than the private return. The UK's historic net deficit on travel services suggests extra capacity may add more to imports than exports. A justified judgement weighs short-run demand effects against long-run supply-side gains and environmental costs, and may argue the decision depends on whether capacity is used for business and inbound travel and on carbon policy.

Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 16 marks; Evaluation up to 9 marks. The same levels apply to option (a) and option (b).
Levels (Knowledge, Application, Analysis):
Level 1 (1-4 marks): Some relevant knowledge, often definitions only; little application to the extracts or the wider economy; analysis is descriptive or confused.
Level 2 (5-8 marks): Accurate knowledge with some relevant application to the extracts; one or two chains of reasoning developed but partial or one-sided; diagrams may be present but are not fully explained.
Level 3 (9-12 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the extracts and to real-world examples; several developed chains of reasoning across micro and macro issues, with appropriate diagrams; some synoptic links between themes.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): Precise, wide-ranging knowledge applied throughout to the data and well-chosen examples; fully developed, logical chains of reasoning with accurate, integrated diagrams; clear synoptic links between microeconomic and macroeconomic effects.
Levels (Evaluation):
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Evaluation is generic or asserted; little reference to the evidence; any conclusion is unsupported.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): Evaluation is present across the answer and considers alternative outcomes, uses some evidence from the extracts, but is not consistently supported or prioritised.
Level 3 (7-9 marks): Sustained evaluation that weighs arguments using the data, considers magnitude, time period, stakeholders and assumptions, prioritises the most significant factors and reaches a fully justified overall judgement.
A* answer: For (a), draws an accurate externality diagram with a tax, uses PED and the per-passenger design to show why APD is a blunt tool, compares it rigorously with carbon pricing, regulation and a frequent flyer levy, and reaches a justified judgement on effectiveness. For (b), traces AD, multiplier and LRAS effects with diagrams, separates gross from net job creation, considers the current account and net zero conflict, and reaches a judgement that depends on spare capacity, time lags and environmental policy.

questions.prompt: Using Table 1, calculate Norland's real interest rate at the end of 2023 and at the end of 2025. Explain what the change suggests about the stance of monetary policy.
questions.context:
Norland: an energy price shock (illustrative data)

Norland is a fictional high-income economy with a floating exchange rate and an independent central bank with a 2% inflation target. It imports most of the natural gas it uses for heating and electricity generation. Its currency is the Norland dollar (N$).

Table 1: Selected economic indicators for Norland, 2021-2025 (illustrative data)
Year | Wholesale gas price index (2021 = 100) | CPI inflation (%) | Central bank policy rate (%, end of year) | Real GDP growth (%) | Unemployment rate (%) | Current account balance (% of GDP)
2021 | 100 | 2.5 | 0.25 | 6.0 | 4.6 | -1.5
2022 | 290 | 9.0 | 3.00 | 3.8 | 3.9 | -4.0
2023 | 170 | 7.0 | 5.25 | 0.3 | 4.1 | -3.2
2024 | 130 | 2.8 | 4.75 | 0.9 | 4.4 | -2.5
2025 | 125 | 3.2 | 4.00 | 1.1 | 4.8 | -2.2

Table 2: Norland's household energy retail market (illustrative data)
Indicator | 2021 | 2025
Number of household energy suppliers | 48 | 22
Combined market share of the five largest suppliers (%) | 70 | 86
Customers switching supplier each month (% of all customers) | 1.8 | 0.4

Extract A: From shock to squeeze
When wholesale gas prices nearly tripled in 2022 after supply disruption abroad, Norland's import bill jumped and inflation rose to its highest rate in three decades. Firms in energy-intensive industries such as chemicals, glass and ceramics cut output, and some postponed investment. Nominal wages rose by around 6% in 2023, but households' real disposable income fell. The central bank raised its policy rate repeatedly between late 2021 and 2023, arguing that it needed to stop high inflation becoming embedded in wage settlements and expectations. Critics argued that higher interest rates could do nothing about the world price of gas and would only deepen the slowdown.

Extract B: The Energy Price Guarantee
In late 2022 the government capped the unit price that suppliers could charge households and paid suppliers the difference between the capped price and their cost of supplying energy. The guarantee applied to all households regardless of income and cost around 2% of GDP in its first year. It was funded by extra borrowing, and the budget deficit rose to 6% of GDP. The finance minister said the guarantee 'took around three percentage points off peak inflation'. Some economists argued that a scheme targeted at low-income households and those with high energy needs, paid for partly by a windfall tax on energy producers' profits, would have been cheaper and would have kept a stronger incentive for better-off households to cut energy use.

Extract C: Supplier failures
Before 2021, dozens of small suppliers had entered Norland's household energy market, attracted by low wholesale prices and a regulated price cap that left room for profit. Many sold fixed-price deals without buying energy in advance to cover them. When wholesale prices rose above the level allowed by the cap, they made a loss on every customer and 26 suppliers collapsed. Their customers were transferred to larger suppliers, and the cost of around N$2.5 billion was added to all households' bills. The regulator has since introduced tougher capital and hedging requirements for new and existing suppliers. The largest firms say these rules make the market more stable; consumer groups say the market has become less competitive and that customer service has worsened.
questions.mark_scheme:
Marking points:
1 mark for knowledge: real interest rate = nominal interest rate - inflation rate (approximately).
1 mark for 2023: 5.25% - 7.0% = -1.75%.
1 mark for 2025: 4.00% - 3.2% = +0.8%.
Up to 2 marks for explanation: although the nominal policy rate was cut from 5.25% to 4.00%, the real interest rate rose by around 2.55 percentage points, from negative to positive (1 mark); so monetary policy became tighter in real terms, increasing the real cost of borrowing and the real reward for saving, which restrains consumption and investment and helps bring inflation back towards target (1 mark). Credit a valid point that using current rather than expected inflation is only an approximation, or that a positive real rate is consistent with the rise in unemployment to 4.8%.

questions.prompt: With reference to Extract A and Table 1, examine, using an AD/AS diagram, the likely effects of the 2022 rise in wholesale gas prices on Norland's real GDP and price level.
questions.context:
Norland: an energy price shock (illustrative data)

Norland is a fictional high-income economy with a floating exchange rate and an independent central bank with a 2% inflation target. It imports most of the natural gas it uses for heating and electricity generation. Its currency is the Norland dollar (N$).

Table 1: Selected economic indicators for Norland, 2021-2025 (illustrative data)
Year | Wholesale gas price index (2021 = 100) | CPI inflation (%) | Central bank policy rate (%, end of year) | Real GDP growth (%) | Unemployment rate (%) | Current account balance (% of GDP)
2021 | 100 | 2.5 | 0.25 | 6.0 | 4.6 | -1.5
2022 | 290 | 9.0 | 3.00 | 3.8 | 3.9 | -4.0
2023 | 170 | 7.0 | 5.25 | 0.3 | 4.1 | -3.2
2024 | 130 | 2.8 | 4.75 | 0.9 | 4.4 | -2.5
2025 | 125 | 3.2 | 4.00 | 1.1 | 4.8 | -2.2

Table 2: Norland's household energy retail market (illustrative data)
Indicator | 2021 | 2025
Number of household energy suppliers | 48 | 22
Combined market share of the five largest suppliers (%) | 70 | 86
Customers switching supplier each month (% of all customers) | 1.8 | 0.4

Extract A: From shock to squeeze
When wholesale gas prices nearly tripled in 2022 after supply disruption abroad, Norland's import bill jumped and inflation rose to its highest rate in three decades. Firms in energy-intensive industries such as chemicals, glass and ceramics cut output, and some postponed investment. Nominal wages rose by around 6% in 2023, but households' real disposable income fell. The central bank raised its policy rate repeatedly between late 2021 and 2023, arguing that it needed to stop high inflation becoming embedded in wage settlements and expectations. Critics argued that higher interest rates could do nothing about the world price of gas and would only deepen the slowdown.

Extract B: The Energy Price Guarantee
In late 2022 the government capped the unit price that suppliers could charge households and paid suppliers the difference between the capped price and their cost of supplying energy. The guarantee applied to all households regardless of income and cost around 2% of GDP in its first year. It was funded by extra borrowing, and the budget deficit rose to 6% of GDP. The finance minister said the guarantee 'took around three percentage points off peak inflation'. Some economists argued that a scheme targeted at low-income households and those with high energy needs, paid for partly by a windfall tax on energy producers' profits, would have been cheaper and would have kept a stronger incentive for better-off households to cut energy use.

Extract C: Supplier failures
Before 2021, dozens of small suppliers had entered Norland's household energy market, attracted by low wholesale prices and a regulated price cap that left room for profit. Many sold fixed-price deals without buying energy in advance to cover them. When wholesale prices rose above the level allowed by the cap, they made a loss on every customer and 26 suppliers collapsed. Their customers were transferred to larger suppliers, and the cost of around N$2.5 billion was added to all households' bills. The regulator has since introduced tougher capital and hedging requirements for new and existing suppliers. The largest firms say these rules make the market more stable; consumer groups say the market has become less competitive and that customer service has worsened.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Short-run aggregate supply shifts with changes in costs of production such as energy and raw materials. A rise in costs shifts SRAS to the left, causing cost-push inflation and lower real output (stagflation). Energy price rises also reduce real disposable income and may affect AD.
Application: The gas price index rose from 100 to 290 in 2022 (+190%); inflation rose from 2.5% to 9.0%; real GDP growth slowed from 6.0% to 3.8% in 2022 and 0.3% in 2023; energy-intensive firms cut output and postponed investment; real disposable income fell; the current account deficit widened from 1.5% to 4.0% of GDP as the import bill rose.
Analysis: Diagram: SRAS1 shifts left to SRAS2 with AD unchanged; the price level rises from P1 to P2 and real output falls from Y1 to Y2. Chain 1: energy is an input for almost all firms, so higher gas prices raise average costs across the economy; firms raise prices and cut output, giving cost-push inflation and slower growth. Chain 2: the shock also lowers AD, because households spend more on imported gas and have less to spend on domestic output (falling real incomes reduce consumption), firms postpone investment and imports rise, so AD may shift left, reinforcing the fall in real GDP while partly offsetting the price rise. Second-round effects: wage rises of around 6% could shift SRAS further left if a wage-price spiral develops.
Evaluation: Real GDP growth stayed positive in 2022 (3.8%), suggesting strong recovery-led demand and a time lag in the effect; the larger slowdown came in 2023 when interest rates also rose, so it is hard to separate the effects. The Energy Price Guarantee reduced the rise in measured inflation by around three percentage points, limiting the shift in SRAS faced by households. The effect depends on energy intensity of output and how far firms had hedged. The shock was temporary: the gas index fell back to 125 by 2025, so SRAS may shift back, though LRAS may be damaged if postponed investment is never made.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 6 marks; Evaluation up to 2 marks.
Levels (Knowledge, Application, Analysis):
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated knowledge with little or no use of the data or context; analysis is absent or a list of assertions; any diagram is inaccurate or not used.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some reference to the data; one or two chains of reasoning that are partly developed; diagram broadly accurate but not fully integrated.
Level 3 (5-6 marks): Precise knowledge applied consistently to the context and figures; two clear, logical and well-linked chains of reasoning; accurate diagram fully explained and integrated where required.
Levels (Evaluation):
Level 1 (1 mark): A generic or asserted evaluative comment.
Level 2 (2 marks): A developed, supported evaluative point that is applied to the context (for example magnitude, time period or what the outcome depends on).
A* answer: Draws an accurate AD/AS diagram with SRAS shifting left, quotes the 190% rise in gas prices, the jump in inflation and slower growth, explains a second chain on falling real incomes and AD, and evaluates using the time lag, the price guarantee and whether second-round wage effects occurred.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Oligopoly: a market dominated by a few large firms with interdependence, high concentration and barriers to entry. Concentration ratio. Consequences may include higher prices, tacit collusion, non-price competition, reduced choice and lower allocative efficiency, but also economies of scale, financial stability and dynamic efficiency.
Application: Suppliers fell from 48 to 22; the five-firm concentration ratio rose from 70% to 86%; switching fell from 1.8% to 0.4% of customers a month (a fall of around 78%); 26 suppliers collapsed; N$2.5 billion of failure costs were added to all bills; tougher capital and hedging rules have been introduced; consumer groups report worse customer service.
Analysis: Higher concentration and new regulatory barriers to entry give the large suppliers more market power; with fewer rivals and interdependence, the incentive to compete on price is weaker and tacit collusion becomes easier, so prices may settle above marginal cost (allocative inefficiency) and consumer surplus falls. The fall in switching suggests less competitive pressure: suppliers face more inelastic demand from customers who see little benefit in switching, so they can raise margins or reduce service quality (X-inefficiency). Reduced entry may lower dynamic efficiency and innovation in tariffs and smart services. On the other hand, larger suppliers can gain economies of scale in billing, purchasing and hedging, lowering average costs; stronger finances and hedging reduce the risk of further failures, whose costs consumers had to bear (N$2.5 billion), so consumers may gain from stability and lower risk. Many earlier entrants were unsustainable because they did not hedge, so their low prices were not a true benefit.
Evaluation: In many energy markets the retail price is constrained by a regulated cap, so the extent to which suppliers can raise prices is limited; the main consequences may be on service quality and choice rather than price. The 86% CR5 does not show behaviour: competition among five large firms can still be intense. Low switching may reflect the cap making tariffs similar rather than market power. The long-run effect depends on whether the tougher rules become a permanent barrier or allow sound new entrants. Different consumers are affected differently: vulnerable consumers who never switched may lose little, active switchers lose most. Justified judgement required, for example that the main loss is reduced choice and service quality, partly offset by greater security of supply.
Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 8 marks; Evaluation up to 4 marks.
Levels (Knowledge, Application, Analysis):
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context or data; analysis is absent or consists of unconnected assertions.
Level 2 (3-5 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; relevant chains of reasoning that may be incomplete or one-sided; diagrams, if used, may contain minor errors.
Level 3 (6-8 marks): Precise, relevant knowledge applied consistently to the context and data; clear, logical and well-linked chains of reasoning covering more than one side of the issue, supported by accurate diagrams or calculations where relevant.
Levels (Evaluation):
Level 1 (1-2 marks): Evaluation is generic or asserted, with little reference to the context; any judgement is unsupported.
Level 2 (3-4 marks): Balanced evaluation supported by the data and context, weighing the significance of the arguments and reaching a justified judgement.
A* answer: Uses the CR5 rise from 70% to 86%, the fall in suppliers and switching data, analyses market power, tacit collusion and X-inefficiency against economies of scale and financial stability, evaluates the role of the regulated price cap and the costs of earlier failures, and reaches a supported judgement about which consumers lose most.

questions.prompt:
Answer EITHER (a) OR (b). Start your answer by writing (a) or (b).

questions.mark_scheme:
This mark scheme covers both options. Mark the option the candidate has chosen using the indicative content for that option and the shared level descriptors.

OPTION (a): The universal Energy Price Guarantee
Knowledge: External shocks; maximum prices and subsidies; fiscal policy; budget deficit and national debt; universal versus targeted (means-tested) support; windfall taxes; absolute and relative poverty and fuel poverty; government failure; the price mechanism's signalling and rationing functions.
Application: Gas prices up 190% in 2022; the guarantee cost around 2% of GDP and the deficit rose to 6% of GDP (Extract B); it reduced peak inflation by around three percentage points; it applied to all households regardless of income; the alternative was targeted support funded partly by a windfall tax.
Analysis: Benefits: by capping household prices, the guarantee directly reduced measured CPI inflation, lowering the risk of a wage-price spiral and of inflation expectations rising, which may have allowed lower interest rates than otherwise. It protected real disposable income, sustaining consumption and AD and reducing the depth of the downturn. It reduced fuel poverty and protected vulnerable households, and was quick and simple to administer because no means test was needed. Costs: a subsidy that holds price below the market level weakens the price signal, so energy demand stays higher than it would be, increasing imports and the current account deficit and keeping world gas prices high. Universal support gave large transfers to high-income households who use most energy, so it was poorly targeted and expensive; borrowing raised the deficit and debt and debt interest costs at a time of rising interest rates. A targeted scheme with a windfall tax could have lowered the cost and preserved incentives to save energy for most households; a windfall tax on supernormal profits can raise revenue with little effect on output in the short run.
Evaluation: Targeting requires accurate information and creates administrative delays and cliff edges; in a fast-moving crisis speed may matter more than precision. The guarantee was temporary, so the effect on long-term debt sustainability may be small. Windfall taxes may deter future investment in energy supply. The best response also depends on whether the shock was expected to be temporary (the index fell to 125 by 2025) and on fiscal space. Supply-side measures (energy efficiency, domestic renewables) address the root cause but work only in the long run. A justified judgement weighs inflation and equity gains against cost, poor targeting and distorted incentives.

OPTION (b): Raising interest rates in response to imported energy inflation
Knowledge: Monetary policy and the transmission mechanism; the central bank's inflation target and independence; cost-push versus demand-pull inflation; inflation expectations and second-round effects; the Phillips curve; conflicts between objectives; the exchange rate channel.
Application: Inflation rose to 9.0% in 2022 and stayed at 7.0% in 2023; the policy rate rose from 0.25% to 5.25%; growth slowed to 0.3% in 2023 and unemployment rose from 3.9% to 4.8%; nominal wages rose around 6% in 2023; inflation fell to 2.8% in 2024; the real interest rate moved from negative to positive.
Analysis: For: a supply shock first raises the price level, but if workers and firms expect inflation to continue, wage claims and price setting create second-round effects that shift SRAS further left and make inflation persistent; raising rates signals the central bank's commitment and anchors expectations. Higher rates reduce consumption (higher borrowing costs, more incentive to save) and investment, reducing AD and the scope for firms to pass on cost increases. Higher rates also attract hot money, appreciating the currency and lowering the domestic price of imported gas. The low unemployment rate in 2022 (3.9%) suggests the labour market was tight, so there was some demand-pull and wage pressure too. Against: higher rates cannot change the world gas price, so the first-round effect must be accepted; tightening into a supply shock deepens the fall in output and raises unemployment (stagflation); time lags of around 18-24 months mean rates may peak just as the shock fades, so the economy is over-tightened, as the fall in inflation to 2.8% by 2024 might suggest. Higher rates raise mortgage costs, worsening the squeeze on real incomes and inequality, and raise the cost of government debt.
Evaluation: The right response depends on whether expectations were becoming unanchored; persistent 7% inflation in 2023 and 6% wage growth suggest they were at risk. It is difficult to know how much inflation would have fallen anyway as gas prices fell back to an index of 125. The size and speed of tightening matter: 'looking through' a one-off shock may be appropriate if expectations are credible. Fiscal policy (the guarantee) and monetary policy interacted: the guarantee lowered inflation but supported demand. Rising unemployment to 4.8% shows a real cost, but higher inflation would also have harmed real incomes and competitiveness. A justified judgement, for example that some tightening was right to prevent second-round effects but the scale may have been excessive given time lags.

Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 16 marks; Evaluation up to 9 marks. The same levels apply to option (a) and option (b).
Levels (Knowledge, Application, Analysis):
Level 1 (1-4 marks): Some relevant knowledge, often definitions only; little application to the extracts or the wider economy; analysis is descriptive or confused.
Level 2 (5-8 marks): Accurate knowledge with some relevant application to the extracts; one or two chains of reasoning developed but partial or one-sided; diagrams may be present but are not fully explained.
Level 3 (9-12 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the extracts and to real-world examples; several developed chains of reasoning across micro and macro issues, with appropriate diagrams; some synoptic links between themes.
Level 4 (13-16 marks): Precise, wide-ranging knowledge applied throughout to the data and well-chosen examples; fully developed, logical chains of reasoning with accurate, integrated diagrams; clear synoptic links between microeconomic and macroeconomic effects.
Levels (Evaluation):
Level 1 (1-3 marks): Evaluation is generic or asserted; little reference to the evidence; any conclusion is unsupported.
Level 2 (4-6 marks): Evaluation is present across the answer and considers alternative outcomes, uses some evidence from the extracts, but is not consistently supported or prioritised.
Level 3 (7-9 marks): Sustained evaluation that weighs arguments using the data, considers magnitude, time period, stakeholders and assumptions, prioritises the most significant factors and reaches a fully justified overall judgement.
A* answer: For (a), uses the 2% of GDP cost, the three-point inflation effect and the deficit data to weigh the guarantee's macroeconomic stabilisation and equity gains against poor targeting, weakened price signals and fiscal cost, and judges it against a targeted scheme with a windfall tax. For (b), distinguishes first-round from second-round effects of a supply shock, uses Table 1 to assess expectations, the labour market and time lags, analyses the transmission mechanism and exchange rate channel, and reaches a nuanced judgement on whether the scale of tightening was right.
